{{Short description|Method for solving differential equations}}
{{for|the similar method in electromagnetics|Method of moments (electromagnetics)}}
{{technical|date=May 2025}}
In [[applied mathematics]], '''methods of mean weighted residuals (MWR)''' are methods for solving [[differential equation]]s.  The solutions of these differential equations are assumed to be well approximated by a finite sum of test functions <math>\phi_i</math>.  In such cases, the selected method of weighted residuals is used to find the coefficient value of each corresponding test function.  The resulting coefficients are made to minimize the error between the [[linear combination]] of test functions, and actual solution, in a chosen norm.

==Notation of this page==
It is often very important to firstly sort out notation used before presenting how this method is executed in order to avoid confusion.

*<math> u(x) </math> shall be used to denote the solution to the differential equation that the MWR method is being applied to.
*Solving the differential equation mentioned shall be accomplished by setting some function <math> R\left(x,u,u_x,\ldots,\frac{d^n u}{dx^n}\right) </math>  called the "residue function" to zero.
*Every method of mean weighted residuals involves some "test functions" that shall be denoted by <math> w_i </math>.
*The degrees of freedom shall be denoted by <math> a_i </math>.
*If the assumed form of the solution to the differential equation <math> R\left(x,u,u_x,\ldots,\frac{d^n u}{dx^n}\right)=0 </math> is linear (in the degrees of freedom) then the basis functions used in said form shall be denoted by <math> \phi_i </math>.

==Mathematical statement of method==
The method of mean weighted residuals solves <math> R\left(x,u,u_x,\ldots,\frac{d^n u}{dx^n}\right)=0 </math> by imposing that the degrees of freedom <math> a_i </math> are such that:

: <math>\langle R\left(x,u,u_x,\ldots,\frac{d^n u}{dx^n}\right),w_i\rangle =0 </math>

is satisfied. Where the inner product <math> \langle f,g \rangle </math> is the standard function inner product with respect to some weighting function <math> r(x) </math> which is determined usually by the [[basis function]] set or arbitrarily according to whichever weighting function is most convenient. For instance, when the basis set is just the [[Chebyshev polynomials]] of the first kind, the weighting function is typically <math> r(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} </math> because inner products can then be more easily computed using a [[discrete Chebyshev transform|Chebyshev transform]].

Additionally, all these methods have in common that they enforce boundary conditions by either enforcing that the basis functions (in the case of a linear combination) individual enforce the boundary conditions on the original BVP (This only works if the boundary conditions are homogeneous however it is possible to apply it to problems with inhomogeneous boundary conditions by letting <math> u(x)=v(x)+L(x) </math> and substituting this expression into the original differential equation and imposing homogeneous boundary conditions to the new solution being sought to find u(x) that is v(x) where L(x) is a function that satisfies the boundary conditions imposed on u that is known.), or by explicitly imposing the boundary by removing n rows to the matrix representing the discretised problem where n refers to the order of the differential equation and substituting them with ones that represent the boundary conditions.

===Choice of test functions===
The choice of test function, as mentioned earlier, depends on the specific method used (under the general heading of mean weighted residual methods). Here is a list of commonly used specific MWR methods and their corresponding test functions roughly according to their popularity:

*The [[Galerkin method]], which uses the basis functions themselves as test functions or in the more general case of a nonlinear assumed form (where the nonlinearity is in the degrees of freedom) of the solution the Galerkin method uses the test functions: <math> w_i =\frac{\partial u}{\partial a_i} </math>
*The [[pseudospectral method]] which uses the [[Dirac delta functions]] centered at a set of discrete x points <math> x_i </math> and equates to just setting the residue function to zero at those x points.
*The least-squares method uses the test functions: <math> w_i =\frac{\partial R}{\partial a_i} </math>. This method has the effect of minimising the square of the [[Lp space#Special cases|L2-norm]] of the residue function (that is <math> \|{R}\|^2 </math>) with respect to the degrees of freedom <math> a_i </math>.
*The method of moments uses the simple set of test functions <math> x^i </math> and is rarely ever implemented when high degrees of accuracy are required because of computational issues associated with inverting the [[Hilbert matrix]].
